One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be sensitive to these expelled fields, which create a gradient that affects the system's performance. As a result, this technique enables the precise measurement of these microscopic fields. In this research, we employed a superconducting YBa$}_{2}$Cu$}_{3}$O$}_{7-$\delta$ (1-2$\mu$m thick) plate in a Mach-Zehndler atomic interferometry setup to clearly distinguish between the expelled field near the superconductor's surface and the field farther away. By varying the superconductor's temperature, we could alter the strength of the expelled field, which resulted in atomic signal degradation. However, further degradation was found to be unavoidable due to non-superconducting properties of the material. To overcome this issue, we thickened the superconductor to 100 nm and observed a significant improvement in atomic signal quality. Ultimately, we achieved the most precise measurement of expelled magnetic field strength using a superconducting material, with an accuracy of 10^-12 N/kg and a scale factor of 10^-10 N/kg/m. This achievement paves the way for utilizing atomic interferometry to investigate various superconducting materials' electromagnetic properties.
